## Working out each component

**Y3 is bit 3.**
- In task X4-Y3-Z4, the only yellow outputs are 0100 1001, 0100 0100 and 1001 0100.
- These are exactly the inputs where bit 3 is 0 in both stimuli. Every green input has a 1 in bit 3 somewhere.
- No other bit separates yellow from green cleanly. For example, 1110 0000 is green, which rules out bits 1, 2 and 4.

**Y2 is bit 4.**
- In task X4-Y2-Z2, the output is blue exactly when bit 4 is 0 in both stimuli. Otherwise it is red.

**Y1 is bit 1.**
- In task X2-Y1-Z4, the output is green exactly when bit 1 is 0 in both stimuli. Otherwise it is yellow.
- Bit 2 fails as an alternative: 0100 1100 is yellow even though bit 2 is the same in both stimuli.

**X4 has two possibilities.**
- X4 is "neither is 1": then Z2 gives blue when true, and Z4 gives yellow when true.
- X4 is "at least one is 1": then Z2 gives red when true, and Z4 gives green when true.

**X2 depends on X4.**
- In task X2-Y1-Z4, yellow means "at least one 1 in bit 1".
- If X4 is "neither", Z4 gives yellow when true, so X2 is "at least one".
- If X4 is "at least one", Z4 gives green when true, so X2 is "neither".
- Both options keep X2 different from X4, so both fit.

**X3 has two possibilities.**
- In tasks X3-Y3-Z2 and X3-Y3-Z1, the output depends on whether bit 3 is 1 in both stimuli.
- X3 is either "both are 1" or "not both are 1", with Z1 and Z2 adjusted to match. Neither choice affects the new task.

**X1 and Z3 are linked.**
- In task X1-Y3-Z3, the output is green when bit 3 is the same in both stimuli and blue when it differs.
- Either X1 is "both are the same" and Z3 gives green when true and blue when false.
- Or X1 is "exactly one is 1" and Z3 gives blue when true and green when false.

## What this means for X2-Y1-Z3

Combining the two X2 options with the two Z3 options gives only two distinct predictions:
- **Option P:** green when bit 1 is 0 in both stimuli, otherwise blue.
- **Option Q:** blue when bit 1 is 0 in both stimuli, otherwise green.

I checked both options against all the known tasks. Nothing rules either one out: all the X versions stay distinct, and all the Z versions stay distinct. So the answers are **not determined**.

I am predicting with Option P, which is a coin flip between the two.

| Input | Bit 1 in both stimuli | Prediction (Option P) |
|---|---|---|
| 1. 0110 0100 | both 0 | green |
| 2. 0101 0010 | both 0 | green |
| 3. 0100 0011 | both 0 | green |
| 4. 1000 0000 | not both 0 | blue |
| 5. 0001 0011 | both 0 | green |
| 6. 1110 1001 | not both 0 | blue |
| 7. 0010 0010 | both 0 | green |
| 8. 1111 1111 | not both 0 | blue |
| 9. 0111 1101 | not both 0 | blue |
| 10. 0110 1110 | both 0 | green |
| 11. 0011 0011 | both 0 | green |
| 12. 1100 0000 | not both 0 | blue |
| 13. 0101 1001 | not both 0 | blue |
| 14. 1111 0100 | not both 0 | blue |
| 15. 0010 0100 | both 0 | green |
| 16. 0011 0101 | both 0 | green |

Under Option Q, every prediction would swap colour.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: blue, red, green, or yellow. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> green` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is green.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
